lessons.title: The main parts of a tractor
lessons.html:
What a tractor does

A tractor is a power unit. It pulls, pushes, lifts and drives farm implements such as ploughs, planters, sprayers, balers and trailers. To do this it has an engine, a drivetrain, a hydraulic system, a power take-off (PTO) and an operator station.

Main systems

  • Engine: almost always a diesel engine. It makes power by burning fuel.
  • Clutch: connects and disconnects the engine from the gearbox.
  • Gearbox (transmission): gives different speeds and directions.
  • Differential and final drives: send power to the wheels and let them turn at different speeds in corners. A diff lock makes both wheels turn together in mud.
  • Front axle: steers the tractor. On four-wheel-drive (4WD or MFWD) tractors it is also driven.
  • Brakes: stop the tractor. Rear brakes can often be used separately to help turn.
  • Hydraulics: lift and lower implements on the three-point linkage and work cylinders on loaders and tippers.
  • PTO: a spinning shaft at the back that drives implements such as slashers and balers.
  • Electrical system: battery, alternator, starter, lights and instruments.
  • Cab or ROPS: the operator's station with a rollover protective structure.

Two-wheel drive or four-wheel drive

A 2WD tractor drives only the rear wheels. It is cheaper and fine for light work. A 4WD tractor drives the front wheels too, which gives better grip for heavy ploughing and wet lands.

Instruments and the hour meter

The dashboard shows the engine speed, oil pressure and temperature warnings, the fuel level and the hour meter. Tractors are serviced by engine hours, not by kilometres, so always write the hour meter reading on the job card before you start work.

lessons.title: Other farm equipment and safe basics
lessons.html:
Equipment you will see in the workshop

Tractor mechanics also work on equipment used with tractors and on other farm machines.

EquipmentUse
Plough and disc harrowTurning and breaking up soil
PlanterPlanting maize, soya and other seed in rows
Boom sprayerSpraying crops
Slasher (bossiekapper)Cutting grass and bush, driven by PTO
BalerMaking hay bales
Front-end loaderLifting and moving soil, manure and bales
TrailerCarrying loads on the farm and road

Implement connections

Implements connect in three main ways: the three-point linkage (two lower arms and a top link), the drawbar (a pin for trailed equipment), and the PTO shaft. Hydraulic hoses connect with quick couplers. Some modern implements also have electrical or data plugs.

Safety basics around tractors

  • The PTO is very dangerous. It can grab loose clothing and pull a person in within a second. Keep guards in place and never step over a turning shaft.
  • Tractors can roll over on slopes and riverbanks. The ROPS and seatbelt save lives; never remove the ROPS.
  • Never start a tractor from the ground. It may be in gear and run over you.
  • Lower implements to the ground before working on the tractor.
  • Only one person on a tractor unless there is a proper passenger seat.

Reading the operator's manual

Every tractor has an operator's manual and a workshop or service manual. The operator's manual shows controls, daily checks and service intervals. The workshop manual has repair steps, specifications and torques. Always use the right manual for the model and serial number.

Key points

  • A tractor has an engine, drivetrain, hydraulics, PTO, electrics and an operator station.
  • The differential lets wheels turn at different speeds; the diff lock locks them.
  • Implements connect by three-point linkage, drawbar and PTO.
  • Keep PTO guards on and never remove the ROPS.
  • Use the correct manual for the tractor model.
